Unlike Raiders of the Lost Ark, which -with the exception of its cosmic finale- - relied primarily on dazzling stuntwork for its thrills and chills, many of the key sequences in the second Indiana Jones adventure were made possible only through the employment of elaborate visual effects. From miniature airplanes and mine cars to large-scale lava and water effects, the cinemagicians of Industrial Light and Magic stretched the limits of their experience and expertise to produce some 140 effects shots for the consummate cliffhanger. Three-time Oscarwinning effects supervisor Dennis Muren discusses the project in detail, aided and abetted by numerous members of his highly-specialized team. Article by Robert P. In their first collaborative effort, director Steven Spielberg and producer George Lucas gave their large and ever-growing audience Raiders of the Lost Ark-an unabashed return to the days of the Saturday afternoon B-movie matinee cram-packed with adventure, mysticism, terror and sometimes even whimsy. Audiences went wild with delight. Now the two high-rolling filmmakers have provided moviegoers with another mini-trip to the fountain of youth-bringing back Raiders' archaeologistadventurer-hero in Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom. Where Raiders, set in 1936, saw the inimitable Dr. Jones overcome Nazi schemes and cosmic disasters in a quest for the lost Ark of the Covenant, the new Indiana Jones is a prequel set in 1935 in the Far East. Instead of Nazis, Jones' antagonists this time are the nefarious leaders of a secret Thuggee cult in India, who practice rituals of human sacrifice and use childslave labor in lava-rimmed mine shafts to search for the lost sacred Sankara stones. Harrison Ford returns in the title role, joined this time by two traveling companions- Kate Capshaw as Willie Scott, a moneyhungry cabaret performer, and Ke Huy Quan as Short Round, a feisty orphaned waif more or less permanently attached to Jones. Overshadowing all, however, are the film's action scenes -heightened immeasurably by some very special special effects produced at Industrial Light and Magic, Lucasfilm's inhouse effects facility. "This show looks much bigger than Raiders," said three-time Oscar-winning visual effects supervisor Dennis Muren. "It is very much like the difference between Star Wars and The Empire Strikes Back. There is an enormous difference in the scope of it and all the places they went. There are a lot of big sets, one after another, and you see more in the frame. All of this is part of the ongoing creative process that Steven Spielberg uses, and it makes for such neat movies. Steven is learning all the time as he is doing it; and that is what is happening here, too. This is a great, action-packed film." Muren had just finished work on Return of the Jedi and was taking a bit of time off when shooting on Indiana Jones began in the island nation of Sri Lanka-followed by three months on stage at EMI Elstree, outside London. During principal photography, Muren - along with effects art director Joe Johnston -shuttled back and forth between London and Lucasfilm's Marin County home base, supervising plate photography and gearing up for the postproduction effects effort. Indiana Jones and Star Trek III thus advanced simultaneously, each with its own dedicated camera crews and effects technicians. "The main challenge on this show," said Warren Franklin, ILM's production supervisor during Indiana Jones, and now general manager of the facility, "was the diversity of effects required. It went from full-scale sets to very tiny miniature caves, so there was an abundance of different technical and logistical things that had to be worked out. And they had to be worked out very quickly and under a very tight schedule. I think this film was a real step forward for the whole facility. We took on water effects, fire effects, things we had never tried to do before. It was not as much work-in number of shots-as Return of the Jedi, but there was more diversity." Although there are many audience-perceived similarities between Indiana Jones and Raiders, there is a major difference in that, except for the opening-of-the-ark sequence, Raiders was more oriented toward death-defying stunts than it was toward special effects. Indiana Jones, on the other hand, while more outwardly grounded in reality, is a veritable treasure-trove of cinematic magic. The initial script for Indiana Jones was delivered to ILM just as the facility was finishing up on Jedi. Muren, Franklin and Johnston reviewed the script in detail, broke it down into possible effects sequences and then developed recommendations on whether particular ideas- at this point, the film was still in the idea stage as far as actual sequences went-should be conveyed with physical effects, miniatures or opticals, what the respective costs might be, and whether the idea was cinematically sound in the first place. These recommendations were then presented to Lucas and Spielberg, executive producer Frank Marshall and associate producer Kathleen Kennedy in several initial storyboard conferences. First the ideas were fleshed out into often spectacular sequences, then necessarily reduced to something that could actually be done with the amount of time and money available. "Many effects just came from Steven's imagination," Franklin explained. "There were things he wanted to see happen, and whether they were done as an effect or practically was a matter of budget and feasibility. He imagined everything that he wanted done, and then it was broken down - 'ILM will do this, and this will be done in England'-and it just went from there, with everyone feeding everyone else's imagination." Some sequences were dropped and others added or expanded. A minor mine car escape became a chase of major proportions in the final film. An aerial dogfight that had most of the principals very excited was ultimately dropped as too costly and impractical. Other sequences which could have been very laborintensive were reevaluated and either simplified or streamlined. One such involved Indy's escape by auto from the Club Obi Wan in Shanghai. We brought the car and our principal players onto the ILM stage and the whole sequence was shot very simply, using lots of smoke and flashing lights. By not stopping the lens down very much, we had very little depth of field - which is what we were after-because all the out-of-focus backgrounds helped to camouflage the fact that we weren't actually using street footage." Devising the various rigs required fell under the purview of supervising stage technician Patrick Fitzsimmons. "We called in Ed Raymond because of his mechanical expertise, and we ended up building twenty-foot diameter spinning light rigswagon wheels - that had as many as twenty or thirty lights opposing. With the car in the middle of the stage, we'd have a spinning light rig three-quarters of the way back and one to the front. With all kinds of dimmers and switchable items, that gave you the idea that this car was moving through all these tight streets with all these different highlights of things whizzing by. We also took a spinning rig and painted sheets of foam core to look like scenery, cut little holes in them, backlit them to look like windows and had them spinning around in the back of the sideways shots so it would look like they were actually driving down these streets. It was very theatrical, but the whole film has that kind of theatrical look to it." Having eluded their pursuers, Indy, Willie and Short Round board a Ford Trimotor cargo plane bound for India. Since only part of the required aerial footage could be obtained with the vintage aircraft procured for the show, the Trimotor flying scenes were augmented at ILM with miniatures and motion control photography. The model aircraft, nearly three feet long and intricately detailed, was constructed by modelmakers Mike Fulmer and Ira Keeler. Originally intended for use in the later-discarded dogfight sequence, the craft was actually overbuilt considering the limited use to which it was ultimately put. A full-size cockpit was also constructed-mainly by Lance Brackett, Ed Raymond and Dave Childers-and mounted on innertube-like bladders whose pressures could be controlled to simulate movement in the air. At Dennis Muren's behest, optical supervisor Bruce Nicholson and his staff devoted considerable effort to refining the cockpit footage so it would be as real as possible. "In our previous films," said Nicholson, especially the space films, the cockpit shots have always been real sharp. That's the easiest way to make sure the mattes will fit. In Indy, we used a new out-of-focus technique with our mattes, even putting foreground subjects - those closest to the camera - out of focus. When Indy is in the cockpit looking out at something, we would put him out of focus so that your attention is drawn toward the object that he's looking at, which is in focus. The only potential problem that you get into is if you have more than one subject, like a cockpit and another plane flying around which you want to be sharp and which is matted into a background. You want to put the cockpit out of focus but you want that plane to be sharp; and both of those mattes have to be run with a background. You then have the problem of not being able to put one out of focus without putting the other out of focus. As a result, the shots we attempted were mostly two-element shots." "Most places I've worked," commented optical camera operator John Ellis, "they do a bluescreen shot, and if they've gotten rid of the matte lines and gotten the color straight, they're done. But here they go a step further and really try to make it part of the environment. Dennis will say: 'Well, that looks good. Now let's make it look natural.' And that's the big difference. In real life, if you were looking out a cockpit window, the cockpit itself would be out of focus because you'd be focusing on the mountains or whatever else was out there. So that's what we did on the cockpit shots. It's very tricky because the matte has to be out of focus to exactly the same degree as the live-action -otherwise the edges will not match. But that's what makes the shot really work, and that's what makes working on a show like this so great. Dennis and Steven are always striving for perfection; and little by little, they're doing away with the conventions that everyone knows don't look right but are generally accepted." En route to its destination, the Trimotor passes over the Great Wall of China-a flawlessly conceived and executed shot that belies its miniature origin. Not only was the aircraft itself a miniature, but so was the Great Wall, a large-scale forced perspective landscape constructed in the ILM modelshop. Since the shot was scheduled for late in the production, and since ILM's motion control rigs were then overloaded with Star Trek material, Dennis Muren opted to farm the scene out to Dream Quest Images-an up-and-coming effects facility which had previously handled some of the ILM overflow from E.T. The miniature aircraft and set were shipped to Dream Quest's Culver City headquarters, with Muren and Lorne Peterson flying down to supervise the setup. Dream Quest programmer Michael Bigelow devised the flowing air-to-air simulation over the Great Wall and also the flight trajectory of the Trimotor. Photographed separately by Hoyt Yeatman, plane and landscape elements were optically combined at Dream Quest and the results shipped back to ILM. "The Great Wall was shot in smoke," said Muren, "with the entire thing backlit to look like early morning. The plane was intentionally made to crab across the background, not in a straight line as everyone would expect. The air-to-air was duplicated on both elements. Dream Quest did a great job. They didn't balk at trying anything, and they delivered the shot when they said they would." The scene, originally intended as background imagery for an animated route map was found sufficiently impressive that it was ultimately left intact for much of its running time, with the map

dissolved in over only its final moments. With the Trimotor abandoned by its crew, Indy takes the controls- without a hint as to how to actually pilot it. A mountaintop looms up before him, and the aircraft's landing gear skims the snowy summit. "At first," said modelshop supervisor Lorne Peterson, "the plan was to have the mountain totally covered in snow, but by the time they got around to shooting the cockpit POVs somewhere up in the Sierras, a lot of the snow had melted. As a result, we had to build a miniature that looked pretty much the same. So up on the roof, we created a whole mountaintop with coal. You can get gigantic pieces of it- maybe two feet square-and hack away at it, and it has that really nice fractured look that granite has, but in smaller scale. So we built this mountain and then covered it with baking soda and microballoons. Then we rigged up a wire so that the plane would come in and just skim the top and the wheels would spin and the snow would fly. It was a pretty hot shot." Suddenly aware that, on top of everything else, the Trimotor is also out of fuel, Indy and his companions have no alternative but to bail out- in an inflatable rubber raft. As the raft lands, plummeting them down a snowy hillside, the aircraft crashes into a mountain behind them. Originally, the three-foot miniature was to have been sacrificed. Fabricated from thin sheets of corrugated aluminum over an inner structure of brass, it had been given a deliberately weakened styrene nose section designed to collapse on impact. Upon further consideration, however, it was decided to build a second model half the size of the first in order to avoid a mountain-building project of major proportions. As it was, Peterson and his crew still had to construct a mountain range about twenty feet across by twelve feet deep. Though the simplest approach would have been to rig a pair of wires and fly the small-scale Trimotor right into the mountain, Muren feared that after impact the wires might still hold up parts of the debris, ruining the shot. It was therefore decided to construct a five-foot-long pneumatic ram that would pull the plane into the mountain, crushing the fuselage and collapsing the wings. "In the beginning of the shot, we did use wires to fly the plane," said Muren, "but just before it hits, we jump-cut to the plane being pulled into the mountain by the ram. Since the plane was out of fuel, we didn't think it should explode on impact and so that's the way we shot it. Later though, after cutting the shot in, Steven and George thought it needed to explode in order to keep the action moving. By this time, however, it was too late to rebuild the set and restage the crash. So we went with what we had and optical matted in one of our stock explosions." Ecstatic that they have somehow escaped unscathed, the unwilling tobogganers have time for only a quick sigh of relief before their raft shoots out over a cliff and down into a gorge hundreds of feet deep. "The scene where the raft goes over the cliff was shot somewhere in Idaho," said Muren, and we had to do a matte painting around it because in the actual shot there were houses and a city in the upper part of the frame. Since the plate was photographed with a very long lens and there was a lot of aerial haze, it turned out to be quite difficult getting our painting to match into it, and we were also trying to work in a tilt." In a subsequent shot, the raft crashlands into a river far below and, finally in its element, passes through a series of white water rapids before drifting to a stop. Greeted by a silent holy man, the adventurous trio is guided to a small Indian village. Although most of the village scenes were filmed on a set constructed in Sri Lanka, the artistry of the ILM matte department was required for a pair of vastly different establishing shots. "We had two shots of the village," explained matte artist Christopher Evans, "one where it's desolate and one where it's alive and active. Early on, they called for a shot where Indy, Willie and the boy are walking down a hill toward the village, and the village is in total desolation, as is the landscape around it. Everything is dead, and there are no children. That scene was actually shot on location, but everything was alive, so my job was to repaint the entire scene with dead foliage. It was like I had Agent Orange on my brush. Then the plate was timed a little bit redder so everything looked brown and parched. Finally, some smoke elements were shot separately and exposed into the village area so it looked as though smoke was coming from little fires in the village." Matte painting supervisor Michael Pangrazio did the 'live' village at the end of the film.iThey needed a shot of the village because evidently it was an add-on in the script. They were rough-cutting the movie and felt they needed an additional establishing shot. So we went out to George Lucas' ranch, which has a lot of acreage, and looked around for a proper location. We went up on a hill and set up our camera in the morning and brought in a bunch of flats to represent building faces. Some of them were pretty big-twenty feet long by seven or eight feet high-and three of them had black doorways painted in. Up close, it looked pretty silly, but from our camera position, which was quite a ways away, it was fine. We had sheets hanging out on clotheslines, flapping in the breeze, and about twenty people dressed in Indian costumes just walking around. Once we got the latent image plate, I worked on the painting for quite a while-Chris helped on it a bit, too-and then optical did a tilt-up on our composite so that as Indy and the others enter the bottom of the frame and walk down the trail, the camera follows them down to reveal the village." Pangrazio, Evans and fellow matte artists Frank Ordaz and Caroleen Green produced some twenty matte paintings for Indiana Jones. A fair number of them were used to represent the child maharaja's castle as seen from various perspectives. Depending upon the extent to which the painting dominated the frame, these and other Indiana Jones matte shots were composited either on the matte camera or in optical. "Unless they're doing it as a latent image shot, they have to either front- or rear-project or camera bipack the live-action plate on their matte stand," explained Bruce Nicholson. "The problem is that there's a contrast difference between taking a plate and rephotographing it on 5247 stock-which is what they do-and recompositing from interpositives to dupe negative, which is what we do. As a result, if the plate takes up a large part of the frame, it's difficult for them to get a quality image. In those cases, we'll normally composite the shot. If the full-frame plate image is reduced down to fit a small area, however, they can usually get by just fine on the matte stand." In several cases, optical was given latent precomposites from the matte camera, to which they added bluescreen elements or other forms of enhancement. "We added flying bats to several of the paintings," Nicholson continued, "just to get some movement into them. Actually they weren't bats, but birds. The main unit had shot a lot of real bats on location in Sri Lanka, and Dennis and I looked at that footage and it was really interesting because they looked more like birds than I expected. Usually when you think of bats you think of wings moving very fastfaster than a bird would moves its wings, anyway-but, in fact, that wasn't the case in the footage we saw. So what we did was go out and shoot birds-backlit against the sky without too many clouds in it. We could then use the sky like a blue screen and make high-contrast mattes from these birds. And it was the mattes themselves that we put into the paintings. Since the birds are just silhouetted against the sky anyway, that was really all we needed. We did have to work with them a little bit, though. When you extract high-contrast mattes, some of the blurred edges will turn into grain. By putting them slightly out of focus or flashing them a little, it really cut down on the apparent grain problem." Matte cameraman Craig Barron was particularly pleased with one shot in which Shorty is seen standing on a balcony in the maharaja's castle at sunset. "Almost the entire shot was a painting that had been done in advance-which is very unusual for a matte shot. Normally the live-action is photographed before anything else is done. In this case, though, Michael Pangrazio painted the temple, courtyard and front balcony first. We then shot a thin-exposure black-and-white line-up clip of the painting. By inserting the line-up clip-which is easy to see throughinto the viewfinder of a VistaVision plate camera, we were able to position the live-action boy into the balcony area. We were on scaffolding with our widest angle lens, shooting down on the far side of the sound stage. I don't think we could have gotten the boy much smaller if we'd tried. By placing a matte or holdout-in this case, black paint on glass with the edges in focus-between the live-action boy and the camera, we were able to 'drop in' the exposure of the boy using latent image. The boy also casts a shadow on a piece of foamcore which we painted orange to match the temple walls. That gave us a

VistaVision precomposite which was then sent to optical for some additional flying bat elements and a reduction to anamorphic format." A hazy, backlit long shot of the castle is one of the film's most beautiful and uncharacteristic matte paintings. After a disappointing attempt to render and photograph the scene via traditional means, Pangrazio opted for a new approach. "I took a drawing we had of the castle and projected it onto a big piece of eight-foot long foam core, cut out all the little turrets and put in pieces of wire for the spindles and little rails like tank tread at the top. So it was like a flat-black mockup of this castle. We found a location up in the hills around here, pounded two big two-by-fours into the ground about fifteen or twenty feet in front of the camera. Then we propped this cutout up against the sky and shot it while the sun was setting behind it. That was kept as a latent image. Then later we set up a pane of glass, rotoed out the basic shape of the castle, and I added a few details to the sides of the castle and put in all kinds of flash tones to create aerial haze throughout. The painting itself looked ridiculously bad-just brush strokes that end in a black sky. But on film, I think it's one of the best things I've done." When Indy and his friends make their way into the subterranean temple-a cavernous interior set constructed at EMI Elstree-they discover an elaborate sacrificial altar where the villainous demagogue Mola Ram is preparing to offer up a victim to the goddess, Kali. Peripheral to the altar area is a crescentshaped fissure of molten lava, represented on the live-action stage by a ten-foot-deep pit with red-gelled lights upturned from below. For a majority of the scenes, where the chasm itself was out of frame, these lights and some attendant steam generators were sufficient to suggest the boiling magma. About a dozen shots, however-from five or six different angles-did call for the lava to be on view, and for these the plan was to add the molten effect optically in postproduction. Exactly what that effect would be, though, had not yet been determined. "What we ended up using," explained Muren, "was a mixture of glycerine and water that we lit from below with gelled lights. Our only other plausible alternative would have been to use something opaque-like white or red paint-light it from the top and pull a matte off it. An advantage to that would have been that the paint could splash up and drip on the sides and still retain its color-which wasn't possible with the other approach. Once you broke the surface of the glycerine, you could see instantly what it was. But paint has a sheen to it-any liquid does-and if you blast all that light down onto it, you get a lot of reflections all over the place and it just doesn't look like a natural light source. By bottom-lighting the glycerine, we could get a brilliant, glowing effect that would actually illuminate the set around it. Then we'd throw a lot of opaque plastic chips and things on top so that most of the surface would appear to be black, but through this black you could still see glowing stuff beneath. On film, it looked very much like real lava.i Amusingly, one of the things chief modelmaker Charlie Bailey tried when there was still an expectation of creating lava that could be frontlit was a combination of vanilla pudding and fluorescent dyes. The resultant goop actually came close to being the correct color and viscosity, but did not have quite the right glow and intensity. It was, however, a major attraction for the studio's resident mouse population which would come out of the woodwork at night to dine on the unexpected treat. Glycerine seemed an altogether better choice. But generating an appropriate representation of lava and then compositing it into the fissure was only part of the problem. "In the live-action shots where you could see the bottom of the stage, Steven had lots of smoke and steam coming up. But for the scenes that needed lava, we had to shoot the plates clean in order to get a good edge for our mattes. As a result, we had to go in later and put smoke overlays on everything, which was horrendously difficult to do-getting the values to match up with the liveaction and all." Any residual doubts about the advisability of employing backlit glycerine were quickly dismissed when Muren and his crew got into their second major involvement with lava effects. As of course they should be in all these films, people are sacrificed in the temple. A section of floor opens at the base of the altar and from the extended arms of the statue a cage with a person inside is lowered down a narrow shaft about sixty feet into a swirling vortex of lava. When we started the sequence, Steven wanted us to do the shots of the people in miniature-looking up at their faces as they're lowered down into the pit. So, based on that information, we started out with a radio-controlled puppet figure thirty inches high, which we figured we could sculpt well enough to look real. Phil Tippett was here at the time and he did the puppets, with Tom St. Amand and two or three other people also working on them. Tom did the armatures and Randy Ottenberg did the costumes. Ease Owyeung made the cage. But then, while I was over in England, Steven decided to make all the up-shots real, and so they built about a thirty-foot-high pit and shot it with a really wide-angle lens and actually dropped people down. And it's much better than anything we could have done because it was real and there was steam coming up and it looked terrific. But at that point, we were already locked into this big scale for our miniatures - which ended up working to our advantage even though we had to build an enormous set. The reality of the shots is incredible because everything's almost half-sized. So that also dictated how big the spiral of glycerine needed to be at the bottom. Originally, it wasn't going to spiral; it was just going to be bub bling. But then Steven thought of the idea of a spiral, like a bull's eye-which I thought was a great idea, so I didn't fight it too much. But it did mean complicating the thing enormously." Since the up-angle shots were completed on stage, what was left for ILM were POV shots and the down-angles of the cage being lowered toward the lava vortex. "As originally conceived," Muren continued, the pit was very narrow-just barely wider than the cage, in fact. Much of the action in Indiana Jones centers around the attempt by our intrepid heroes to escape from the temple of doom in a runaway mine car. "The mine car chase was really expanded upon," Warren Franklin commented. "In the original script, they just got in the mine car and ran through the tunnel and got out at the end of it. Only a few key sequences were laid out. Everything in-between was devised by Steven, Joe Johnston, Dennis and Mike McAlister-how it was going to happen and little tricks and situations the characters would get into until the end of the ride. We had basically the same situation with the speeder bike chase in Return of the Jedi. That was a paragraph in the script that became two minutes of screen time involving a hundred effects shots. Almost the same thing happened with the mine car chase. It kept expanding and expanding until it became our showcase piece for the film. So it's often hard when we look at a script to anticipate where things are going to develop-especially working with Steven and George who are both very open about going beyond what is written in the script." In true Lucasfilm fashion, the mine car chase was to be an amalgam of live-action photography and miniature effects, flawlessly blended into a unified whole. "What happens in a normal motorized Nikon," said McAlister, "is that the speed the film attains when it is going through the gate is fast enough so that momentum alone will cause the film to continue moving on even after the sprocket wheel has stopped. One of the challenges involved in matching ILM's miniature footage to Spielberg's already-completed stage photography lay in trying to replicate the shakes and bumps of the live-action camera as it rumbled down the track. The live-action shakes were not unwanted-they added, in fact, a nice documentary flavor to the sequence. On the down side, however, they created a significant problem for ILM since the miniature shots to be intercut with the live-action were, of necessity, smoothly filmed. Dennis Muren realized that to match the live footage, some kind of corresponding shake and jiggle would have to be introduced. Optical camera operator John Ellis took on the assignment. "It was all done on our quad printer. First we'd take each shot and have Don Clark precomposite it on the Anderson printer in fullframe VistaVision. Then, once the shot was okayed by Dennis, Bruce Nicholson or Steven, we would put it on the quad printer, which we use to generate our finished 4-perf composites. Since the top and bottom of the VistaVision frame are not used in the widescreen anamorphic format, we had roughly two-and-athe rides ner h half fields north and two-and-a-half fields south to work with. The idea was to create the shake entirely on the printer. We could have done it stop-motion by raising or lowering the lens between frames, but we wanted a more realistic blurring effect, so we did it while the printer was running. I'd go over to the tower where we have the solenoid motors for our quad printer, and by moving the projector while the camera was running, I'd be able to add shakes and bumps and jiggles with just the right amount of blur and smear. The direction of the move was controlled by a toggle switch and the speed by a variable speed pot. It was just north-south, of course, since we use all the eastwest area when we squeeze down to 4-perf. But everything was all worked out in advance, and I'd have one of the line-up men, or whomever else was available, calling out: 'Shake ... heavy shake... light shake... bounce!' And I would just do it by hand. Some shots took more shake than others and some of them didn't have any shake at all in portions, and then maybe a violent shake in the middle. I had to decide how much of a move to make on each shot; and since I did them all, I soon developed a feel for how much move I had to give it to get a light shake, a medium shake and so on. So that's how we got it to cut together with the live-action." But what happens when it doesn't cut together well? For effects editor Howard Stein, it was a blessing having the primary editorial team right next door. "It's really valuable to have the editors close by because things are changing all the time. have been both difficult and dangerous. The task, therefore, was relegated to the ILM miniatures unit. But 'miniature' proved to be a relative term when it came to executing this effect. Outside, in the ILM parking lot, stage technicians under the supervision of Patrick Fitzsimmons constructed a basic framework for the quarter-scale replica- a giant twenty-five feet wide by thirty feet long and eighteen feet high. Looming over the set was a 1300-gallon water tank-some eight feet in diameter and about six feet in depth-rigged with a pin that could be pulled to tip it over and flood the cave. A kind of double hinge was devised by modelmaker Paul Huston to permit the tank to first open up and then fall forward, instead of just toppling on a single pivot point. Since the tank was to unleash about 11,000 pounds of water against the miniature cave walls -which obviously could not move or buckle when struck by the force-the basic aluminum foil structures had to be sprayed on the backside with a type of roofing urethane and then further reinforced with a foam and lumber superstructure. The floor of the cave was heavy-duty urethane foam spread over a shock-absorbing bed of moist sand. More importantly, the crew dug down three feet into the asphalt and poured concrete piers as if they were constructing a building, In fact, as the set began taking shape, passers-by were heard to comment that they thought ILM had decided to build condominiums on the property. "To stop the tank from destoying the whole set when it fell," said Fitzsimmons, "we connected it to a 45,000-pound rated cable. "Unfortunately, there's not too much you can do about it," Muren commented. "We looked into various ways of thinning water.
